Right, so before they arrive, a quick map of who is coming, because it matters. Paul is the one who talks. He is not rude, he simply fills every silence, so if you want to say something you are going to have to interject, and he will not mind at all. His wife Ann is the opposite. She will say four things all evening and every one of them will be worth hearing, so if there is a lull, ask her something. The two who are coming from Lisbon are new to me as well. And a warning about my brother. He will ask you what you used to earn about twenty minutes in, he asks everybody, and the correct answer is a joke and a change of subject. Nobody expects a number and nobody has ever given him one.

The whole evening has three moments that decide how it goes, and none of them is the middle. The first is the door. You have about forty seconds while the coats are coming off, and one prepared question is worth more than an hour of good intentions. Ask something specific that is not about work and not about the weather. The second is the lull. Every dinner has one, usually after the main course, and everybody feels it and almost nobody fills it, which means the person who does becomes the host of the table for the next ten minutes. Have something ready. A question, not a story. And the third is the exit. Leaving badly undoes a good evening, and leaving well takes one sentence: name a specific thing somebody said, and say you want to hear the rest of it next time. That sentence is the reason people invite you again.

Vivian warns Braulio at the door that Paul talks a great deal and will not mind being interrupted. Braulio asks her what he should do when the table goes quiet after the main course.
